text: Pulau Ubin: The Island Singapore Decided to Keep
Ten minutes by bumboat from Changi Point, Singapore becomes another country.

Granite blocks quarried and shaped on the island by Indian convict labour went into the Horsburgh Lighthouse in 1851; Ubin stone built the Istana in 1869 and went, with Bukit Timah granite, into the Singapore–Johore Causeway in 1923.
It employed more than a hundred men, most of them islanders, and in the 1990s it was still supplying 160 to 180 tons of granite a month — some 30 to 40 percent of Singapore's whole demand.
The figures are stark: 2,028 people at the 1970 census; about 1,000 by 1987; 139 in 2001; and by 2012, just 38 residents in 24 households.
The legend says that when the First World War broke out in 1914, British soldiers came to Ubin to intern the German family who ran a coffee plantation there.
It is also, on the evidence, not true — and the unravelling is the better tale.
In 1967 the People's Association established the Outward Bound School of Singapore on Pulau Ubin, set up by Dr Goh-Keng-Swee.

I slept in the trainees' bunk one night and was woken by loud bangs going off around us; my friend explained, quite matter-of-factly, that they were thunderflashes, which the instructors set off around their trainees.
It was slated for reclamation, and was saved at the very end of 2001, days before the work was due to begin, when a survey revealed how much life the shore held and the public took up its cause.
On the 10th of October 2013 the Energy Market Authority inaugurated the Pulau Ubin Micro-Grid Test-Bed, built by a consortium of Daily Life Renewable Energy and OKH Holdings.

In a written reply in March 2026, the Government reported that in 2025 solar supplied only about 10 percent of the micro-grid's electricity and diesel the remaining 90 percent, and that there were thirteen power trips that year — a long way from the operator's publicity about an island running on sunshine.
The Ubin Project, launched in 2014 with the island's community, carries a promise worth quoting exactly: "We are committed to retain Ubin in its rustic state for as long as possible."

The last villagers, the schoolboys on their solo nights, and a grid that runs an experiment at village scale are all part of the same decision: to keep one place where Singapore can still see its own beginning.
